Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher_Martin:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Fletcher_Martin_Juley_Collection_J0083191_cropped.jpg/250px-Fletcher_Martin_Juley_Collection_J0083191_cropped.jpg)](/wiki/File:Fletcher_Martin_Juley_Collection_J0083191_cropped.jpg)

Fletcher Martin at work in his studio, circa 1945

**Fletcher Martin** (April 19, 1904 – May 30, 1979) was an American painter, illustrator, muralist and educator. He is best known for his images of military life during World War II and his sometimes brutal images of boxing and other sports.

Martin was born in 1904 in [Palisade, Colorado](/wiki/Palisade,_Colorado "Palisade, Colorado"), one of seven children of newspaperman Clinton Martin and his wife Josephine. The family relocated to Idaho and later Washington. By the age of twelve he was working as a printer. He dropped out of high school and held odd jobs such as lumberjack and professional boxer. He served in the U.S. Navy from 1922 to 1926. His artistic skills were largely [self-taught](/wiki/Autodidacticism "Autodidacticism").

Martin worked as a printer in Los Angeles in the late 1920s, and as an assistant to Mexican muralist [David Alfaro Siqueiros](/wiki/David_Alfaro_Siqueiros "David Alfaro Siqueiros") in the early 1930s. He taught at local art schools such as Otis Art Institute.

He won commissions to paint murals for the New Deal's [Section of Painting and Sculpture](/wiki/Section_of_Painting_and_Sculpture "Section of Painting and Sculpture"), including *Mail Transportation* (1938), painted for the San Pedro Federal Building and Post Office in Los Angeles.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Under the [WPA](/wiki/Works_Progress_Administration "Works Progress Administration") he painted a mural study for the [Kellogg, Idaho](/wiki/Kellogg,_Idaho "Kellogg, Idaho") post office titled *Mine Rescue* (1939). Local industrialists objected that it depicted the dangers of mining, while officials of the Mine & Smelt Workers Union praised it. The industrialists prevailed and Martin painted an uncontroversial mural, *Discovery* (1941), depicting the prospector who founded the town.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) The rejected mural study is now in the [Smithsonian American Art Museum](/wiki/Smithsonian_American_Art_Museum "Smithsonian American Art Museum"). Perhaps his most ambitious mural, also done under the WPA, was painted for [North Hollywood High School](/wiki/North_Hollywood_High_School "North Hollywood High School") in Los Angeles. *Legends of Fernandino and Gabrileno Indians* (1937) depicts overlapping scenes of Native American life and ritual, and the world being carried on the backs of giants.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Mine_Rescue_1939_Fletcher_Martin_WPA.jpg/500px-Mine_Rescue_1939_Fletcher_Martin_WPA.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mine_Rescue_1939_Fletcher_Martin_WPA.jpg)

*Study for Mine Rescue* (1939), Smithsonian American Art Museum

As an artist-correspondent for [*Life Magazine*](/wiki/Life_(magazine) "Life (magazine)") during [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Martin made hundreds of sketches of U.S. soldier life. Fourteen of his paintings from the North African campaign were published in the December 27, 1943, issue of *Life*, and brought him national recognition.[[5]](#cite_note-5) Among these was *Boy Picking Flowers, Tunisia*, depicting a young [GI](/wiki/G.I._(military) "G.I. (military)") finding a distraction from war. He also made illustrations of wartime London and the June 1944 [Normandy Invasion](/wiki/Normandy_Invasion "Normandy Invasion").

Martin's paintings often depicted men in conflict. *Trouble in Frisco* (1938, [Museum of Modern Art](/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art")) shows a brawl between [longshoremen](/wiki/Longshoremen "Longshoremen") witnessed through a ship's porthole. *The Undefeated* (1948–49, [St. Petersburg Museum of Fine Arts](/wiki/Museum_of_Fine_Arts_(St._Petersburg,_Florida) "Museum of Fine Arts (St. Petersburg, Florida)")) depicts the 11th round of the June 25, 1948, World heavyweight boxing championship. The title is ironic: its subject is a severely battered [Jersey Joe Walcott](/wiki/Jersey_Joe_Walcott "Jersey Joe Walcott"), collapsed against the referee and about to lose to (an unseen) [Joe Louis](/wiki/Joe_Louis "Joe Louis").[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 1954 he painted a series of illustrations for *[Sports Illustrated](/wiki/Sports_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")* of heavyweight champion [Rocky Marciano](/wiki/Rocky_Marciano "Rocky Marciano") [defending his title](/wiki/Rocky_Marciano_vs._Ezzard_Charles "Rocky Marciano vs. Ezzard Charles") against [Ezzard Charles](/wiki/Ezzard_Charles "Ezzard Charles").[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Many of Martin's most popular works were reproduced as [woodcuts](/wiki/Woodcut "Woodcut"), [lithographs](/wiki/Lithograph "Lithograph") or [silkscreens](/wiki/Silkscreen "Silkscreen"). After the war he taught at the [Art Students League](/wiki/Art_Students_League "Art Students League") Summer School in [Woodstock, New York](/wiki/Woodstock,_New_York "Woodstock, New York"), settled in the town, and began raising a family. He experimented with abstractionism and began painting naïve images of women and children.

During his career he was a visiting instructor or artist-in-residence at the [University of Florida](/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida"), [State University of Iowa](/wiki/State_University_of_Iowa "State University of Iowa"), the [University of Minnesota](/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota"), [San Antonio Art Institute](/wiki/McNay_Art_Museum "McNay Art Museum"), and [Washington State University](/wiki/Washington_State_University "Washington State University").[[8]](#cite_note-8) He received prizes from the [Los Angeles County Museum of Art](/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Art "Los Angeles County Museum of Art") in 1935 (for *Rural Family*) and 1939 (for *A Lad from the Fleet*); the 1947 Lippincott Prize from the [Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts](/wiki/Pennsylvania_Academy_of_the_Fine_Arts "Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts") (for *Dancer Dressing*); and the 1949 Altman Prize from the [National Academy of Design](/wiki/National_Academy_of_Design "National Academy of Design") (for *Cherry Twice*).[[9]](#cite_note-9) He was elected an associate of the National Academy of Design in 1969, and a full academician in 1974.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

> Lots of students get trapped in the effort to be original. After fifty million paintings have been painted you can see that it is impossible to be highly original. There is always precedent. Who would want to be that original anyway? A better intent is to see that one's work is truly one's own — an honest expression of deep personal feelings. The whole history of art, which can't help but affect one, will be filtered through your own personality to produce a sort of original statement.

— Fletcher Martin.

Martin married five times; four marriages ended in divorce. His wives were: first, poet Cecile Boot (married November 1925, divorced ?); second, script writer Henriette Lichtenstein (married 1935, divorced 1941); third, nurse Maxine Ferris (married 1941, divorced 1945); fourth, actress Helen Donovan (married February 1946, with whom he had sons Donovan, Clinton and Robin, divorced 1961); fifth, novelist Jean Sigsbee Small (married 1962).[[11]](#cite_note-11) He had a much-publicized relationship with movie star [Sylvia Sidney](/wiki/Sylvia_Sidney "Sylvia Sidney"),[[12]](#cite_note-12) and painted two portraits of her.[[13]](#cite_note-13) He and Small retired to Guanajuato, Mexico in 1967, where they lived until his death in 1979.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/San_Pedro_Post_Office_Mural.JPG/250px-San_Pedro_Post_Office_Mural.JPG)](/wiki/File:San_Pedro_Post_Office_Mural.JPG)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Boundary_County_Courthouse.jpg/250px-Boundary_County_Courthouse.jpg)](/wiki/File:Boundary_County_Courthouse.jpg)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Fletcher_Martin_Juley_Collection_J0083191_cropped.jpg/250px-Fletcher_Martin_Juley_Collection_J0083191_cropped.jpg)](/wiki/File:Fletcher_Martin_Juley_Collection_J0083191_cropped.jpg)

Fletcher Martin at work in his studio, circa 1945

**Fletcher Martin** (April 19, 1904 – May 30, 1979) was an American painter, illustrator, muralist and educator. He is best known for his images of military life during World War II and his sometimes brutal images of boxing and other sports.

Martin was born in 1904 in [Palisade, Colorado](/wiki/Palisade,_Colorado "Palisade, Colorado"), one of seven children of newspaperman Clinton Martin and his wife Josephine. The family relocated to Idaho and later Washington. By the age of twelve he was working as a printer. He dropped out of high school and held odd jobs such as lumberjack and professional boxer. He served in the U.S. Navy from 1922 to 1926. His artistic skills were largely [self-taught](/wiki/Autodidacticism "Autodidacticism").

Martin worked as a printer in Los Angeles in the late 1920s, and as an assistant to Mexican muralist [David Alfaro Siqueiros](/wiki/David_Alfaro_Siqueiros "David Alfaro Siqueiros") in the early 1930s. He taught at local art schools such as Otis Art Institute.

He won commissions to paint murals for the New Deal's [Section of Painting and Sculpture](/wiki/Section_of_Painting_and_Sculpture "Section of Painting and Sculpture"), including *Mail Transportation* (1938), painted for the San Pedro Federal Building and Post Office in Los Angeles.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Under the [WPA](/wiki/Works_Progress_Administration "Works Progress Administration") he painted a mural study for the [Kellogg, Idaho](/wiki/Kellogg,_Idaho "Kellogg, Idaho") post office titled *Mine Rescue* (1939). Local industrialists objected that it depicted the dangers of mining, while officials of the Mine & Smelt Workers Union praised it. The industrialists prevailed and Martin painted an uncontroversial mural, *Discovery* (1941), depicting the prospector who founded the town.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) The rejected mural study is now in the [Smithsonian American Art Museum](/wiki/Smithsonian_American_Art_Museum "Smithsonian American Art Museum"). Perhaps his most ambitious mural, also done under the WPA, was painted for [North Hollywood High School](/wiki/North_Hollywood_High_School "North Hollywood High School") in Los Angeles. *Legends of Fernandino and Gabrileno Indians* (1937) depicts overlapping scenes of Native American life and ritual, and the world being carried on the backs of giants.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Mine_Rescue_1939_Fletcher_Martin_WPA.jpg/500px-Mine_Rescue_1939_Fletcher_Martin_WPA.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mine_Rescue_1939_Fletcher_Martin_WPA.jpg)

*Study for Mine Rescue* (1939), Smithsonian American Art Museum

As an artist-correspondent for [*Life Magazine*](/wiki/Life_(magazine) "Life (magazine)") during [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Martin made hundreds of sketches of U.S. soldier life. Fourteen of his paintings from the North African campaign were published in the December 27, 1943, issue of *Life*, and brought him national recognition.[[5]](#cite_note-5) Among these was *Boy Picking Flowers, Tunisia*, depicting a young [GI](/wiki/G.I._(military) "G.I. (military)") finding a distraction from war. He also made illustrations of wartime London and the June 1944 [Normandy Invasion](/wiki/Normandy_Invasion "Normandy Invasion").

Martin's paintings often depicted men in conflict. *Trouble in Frisco* (1938, [Museum of Modern Art](/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art")) shows a brawl between [longshoremen](/wiki/Longshoremen "Longshoremen") witnessed through a ship's porthole. *The Undefeated* (1948–49, [St. Petersburg Museum of Fine Arts](/wiki/Museum_of_Fine_Arts_(St._Petersburg,_Florida) "Museum of Fine Arts (St. Petersburg, Florida)")) depicts the 11th round of the June 25, 1948, World heavyweight boxing championship. The title is ironic: its subject is a severely battered [Jersey Joe Walcott](/wiki/Jersey_Joe_Walcott "Jersey Joe Walcott"), collapsed against the referee and about to lose to (an unseen) [Joe Louis](/wiki/Joe_Louis "Joe Louis").[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 1954 he painted a series of illustrations for *[Sports Illustrated](/wiki/Sports_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")* of heavyweight champion [Rocky Marciano](/wiki/Rocky_Marciano "Rocky Marciano") [defending his title](/wiki/Rocky_Marciano_vs._Ezzard_Charles "Rocky Marciano vs. Ezzard Charles") against [Ezzard Charles](/wiki/Ezzard_Charles "Ezzard Charles").[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Many of Martin's most popular works were reproduced as [woodcuts](/wiki/Woodcut "Woodcut"), [lithographs](/wiki/Lithograph "Lithograph") or [silkscreens](/wiki/Silkscreen "Silkscreen"). After the war he taught at the [Art Students League](/wiki/Art_Studen
